How to Remove Images of Yourself from Google Search

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

To remove an image from Google Search for good, you need to act on two levels: the website that hosts the photo and Google's index that displays it. The fastest lasting route is usually getting the site owner to delete the file, then asking Google to refresh its outdated copy; when the owner refuses, Google's personal content policies, copyright notices or a GDPR request can take the image out of results. In Italy the law on personal image rights adds further leverage.

Why a photo keeps appearing even after you ask

Google Images does not store your photo as its own content: it indexes a file that lives on someone else's server and shows a thumbnail with a link to the page. As long as the original file stays online and public, Google will keep finding it, even if you request removal of a single result.

The same picture is often copied across several sites, social profiles, aggregators and scraper pages. Each copy is a separate URL with its own thumbnail, so a reverse image search with Google Lens is the first job: it shows how many copies exist and which pages actually rank for your name. Only after that inventory is it possible to decide, copy by copy, which route fits.

First route: the site owner or the platform

Asking the publisher to delete the image is the most effective step because it removes the source rather than hiding it. Most Italian websites list a contact or a privacy officer, and social platforms have their own reporting flows for photos posted without consent.

A short, factual request works better than a threatening one. It should include:

  • the exact page URL and the direct image URL (right-click, "copy image address");
  • who you are and why the photo concerns you;
  • the legal basis: your right to your own image under art. 10 of the Italian Civil Code and articles 96–97 of the Copyright Law (Legge 633/1941), plus erasure under GDPR art. 17 when the photo is personal data;
  • a reasonable deadline for a reply.

Platforms operating in the EU must also handle notices under the Digital Services Act, giving a reasoned decision and an appeal route, as explained in our article on platform liability after the DSA. Once the owner deletes or replaces the file, Google may still show the old thumbnail for weeks. The Refresh Outdated Content tool lets anyone submit the image URL so Google confirms it is gone and drops it.

Google's own policies for removing photos

When the site ignores you, Google itself will remove photos from Google results in several defined situations, even though the image remains on the original page. These requests are filed through Google's personal content removal forms, and each policy has its own conditions.

Non-consensual explicit or intimate images

Explicit images shared without consent, including synthetic "deepfake" sexual content, are removed from search on request, and Google also tries to filter duplicates. In Italy this conduct is also a crime under art. 612-ter of the Criminal Code, and the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali runs a procedure that allows people who fear an intimate image is about to be published to report it in advance.

Images of minors

Anyone under 18, or a parent or guardian acting for them, can ask Google to remove images of the minor from search results, with limited exceptions for cases of strong public interest. This applies to school photos, sports team pages and family pictures shared by others.

Doxxing and personal information

Images that reveal identity documents, signatures, medical records or contact details combined with threats or harassment fall under Google's personal information policy. The "Results about you" dashboard handles contact details; for images showing such data, the specific removal form is the right channel.

Google removes images under its policies only from search. If the photo is harmful wherever it appears, the request to the site or platform must run in parallel.

Copyright: when you took the photo yourself

If you are the author of the photo, a copyright notice is often quicker than any privacy argument. A selfie, a professional portrait you commissioned with a transfer of rights, or a picture from your company archive used without permission can all be reported through Google's legal removal form for copyright infringement, commonly called the DMCA route.

The notice requires the URLs, a description of the original work and a statement in good faith that the use is not authorised. Google forwards notices to the Lumen database, so the request itself becomes partially public; for sensitive matters this is worth considering. Note also that copyright belongs to the person who took the picture, not to the person portrayed: a photo taken of you by a journalist is protected by their rights, and here the route is personal data or image rights instead.

The right to be forgotten for images

The right to be forgotten applies to images just as it does to text, because a photo that identifies you is personal data. Under GDPR art. 17 and the principle set by the Court of Justice in Google Spain (C-131/12), you can ask Google to delist results for your name when the information is inaccurate, excessive or no longer relevant, and your interest outweighs the public's.

For right to be forgotten images, Google assesses the same factors as for articles: your role in public life, the age of the photo, the context of the page and whether it is journalistic. A twenty-year-old picture from a local event linked to an acquittal is a strong candidate; a recent photo of a company director at an official event is weaker. Our guide to the right to be forgotten in the EU covers what Google really accepts. If Google refuses, a complaint (reclamo) to the Garante or an action before an Italian court are the next steps.

Defamatory or manipulated images

Edited photos, captions falsely linking you to a crime and memes that damage professional reputation may constitute defamation under art. 595 c.p., aggravated when spread online. Removal of defamatory images normally goes through the platform first, with evidence preserved by certified screenshots, and through the courts if the publisher does not cooperate.

Choosing the right route: a quick comparison

The correct channel depends on who owns the image and what it shows. Using the wrong one wastes weeks and can lead to a rejection that later has to be overturned.

SituationBest routeWhat it removes
Site deleted the photo, thumbnail still visibleRefresh Outdated Content toolOld Google copy
Photo you took, used without permissionCopyright notice to Google and hostSearch result and often the file
Intimate image, minor, doxxingGoogle personal content formsSearch result
Outdated or irrelevant photo tied to your nameRight to be forgotten requestResult for name searches in the EU
Defamatory or manipulated imagePlatform notice, then legal actionThe content itself

Many real cases combine two or three of these at once, for example a copyright notice for the original photo plus a delisting request for a news page that reused it.
